strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: representing shape maps as a composition of invertible flow-matching models anchored at a shared Gaussian, which naturally yields bijectivity, high coverage, and representation-agnostic correspondence in a zero-shot fashion once per-shape flows are trained.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across established benchmarks (FAUST, SMAL, SHREC20, Kinect) with sensible metrics (Euclidean, geodesic, Dirichlet, coverage) and comparisons against a broad range of paradigms (KNN, OT, functional maps, ZoomOut, NAM, NDP).

Careful analysis of design choices: ablations over embedding types (Table 1), a direct quantitative comparison against GeomDist/DDIM inversion justifying the flow-matching choice (Table 2), and honest discussion of when FUSE helps (non-aligned features) and when it does not (xyz, already-aligned FMNet features).

New contribution to evaluation infrastructure: an SDF-based FAUST benchmark for cross-representation matching, plus diverse downstream applications (scan fitting/skinning, mesh parametrization, volumetric matching) that demonstrate versatility beyond a single task.
Clear writing, good related-work positioning, and candid limitation discussion (non-smoothness of maps from flow inversion, degradation on raw point clouds).
weaknesses: The method relies on geodesic embeddings computed from a small set of hand-selected landmarks, which constitutes a nontrivial manual prior; the paper does not fully quantify sensitivity to landmark choice or placement errors, and landmark selection on raw scans/point clouds is glossed over.

Flows are trained independently per shape; per-shape training time and computational cost are not reported in the main text, making it hard to assess the practical 'computationally efficient' claim relative to cheaper baselines like plain KNN or FMaps.

Absolute matching accuracy is often behind refinement baselines (ZoomOut, NAM, NDP) on several datasets; FUSE's strongest standalone results come mainly when used as an initialization for these methods, which weakens the 'superior matching accuracy' claim to a degree.

The construction is a relatively direct adaptation of Geometry Distributions [57] to feature space with FM instead of diffusion; while the DDIM-vs-FM ablation is appreciated, the novelty is more architectural than conceptual, and the 'first' claims should be stated more carefully.
Non-smooth maps (high Dirichlet energy) are a known consequence of flow inversion and require a post-hoc MLP smoothing step for parametrization; a principled solution or deeper analysis is missing.

Several experimental details are deferred to supplementary material (volume matching metric, inter-representation analysis), and reproducibility information (code/architecture/training details) is not evident from the main paper.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and simple: composing independently trained invertible flows through a shared Gaussian anchor yields a zero-shot map between shapes, with a clean probabilistic interpretation of feature alignment.

The representation-agnostic formulation is genuinely appealing: matching across meshes, point clouds, SDFs, and volumetric (tetrahedral) data in a single framework is a real practical capability, and the inter-representation experiments (Figure 6) and volumetric comparison (Table 5) are interesting beyond standard benchmarks.

The evaluation spans multiple established datasets (FAUST, SMAL, SHREC20, Kinect) with sensible metrics including coverage and Dirichlet energy, plus ablations on embedding choice (Table 1) and a direct comparison against GeomDist/DDIM (Table 2) that substantiates the design choice of flow matching over diffusion.

Downstream applications (scan fitting/skinning, mesh parametrization, volume matching) demonstrate the representation is not limited to a single task, and the paper is candid about limitations such as the non-smoothness of flow inversion.
The paper is clearly written at a conceptual level, with a well-organized background section that makes the method accessible to readers outside the flow-matching literature.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is thin. The construction is essentially Flow Matching [22,23] applied to embedding distributions, and the closest prior work, GeomDist [57], already represents shapes as distributions bridged through a Gaussian. The two claimed deltas (FM instead of diffusion; embedding distributions instead of coordinates) are incremental, and the authors themselves note FM and diffusion are 'two sides of the same coin' [16], which undercuts the framing of Table 2 as a fundamental contribution.

The method is not as unsupervised or 'zero-shot' as claimed: the geodesic embedding requires a manually selected set of 5-6 landmarks per shape, which is effectively weak supervision and parallels the landmark priors used by axiomatic FMaps variants. The sensitivity to landmark selection and placement is never ablated, yet this is arguably the main driver of accuracy.

The headline results require refinement to be competitive. In Table 3, plain 'Ours' is rarely the best method on accuracy (e.g., NDP and ZO outperform it on FAUST Euclidean/geodesic; KNN-IN-GAUSS beats it on the non-isometric SMAL/SHREC20 accuracy), and the strongest reported numbers come from Ours-ZO/Ours-NAM, which reintroduce the per-pair optimization the paper claims to avoid. The accuracy gap is partially obscured by highlighting coverage, where FUSE is strongest.

Missing computational analysis. The paper claims computational efficiency but never reports per-shape flow training time, inference cost of the ODE integration, or memory footprint, making the efficiency claim unverifiable relative to FMaps/ZO baselines.

No comparison against modern learned/unsupervised shape matching methods (e.g., unsupervised spectral matching [8], Diff3F [13], transformer-based registration [51]). The claim of outperforming data-driven approaches is not supported by the baseline set, which is mostly axiomatic.

Reproducibility concerns: metric normalization is unclear (e.g., Euclidean errors of ~0.03 on FAUST without units or a stated convention), key implementation details (network architecture, number of samples, ODE solver, steps) are deferred or absent, and the SDF benchmark is newly introduced by the authors with no external validation and evaluated only against weak baselines (Table 4, where NDP achieves better coverage and Dirichlet energy).

Presentation quality is below par for a top venue: multiple typos ('architechtures', 'intoduced', 'gedesics', 'reminder of the paper'), inconsistent terminology (KNN-IN-GAUSS vs knn-in-gauss), and metric definitions pushed to the supplementary material.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated representation: recasting shape maps as composition of invertible flows through a shared Gaussian anchor is a fresh, probabilistic alternative to functional maps, OT, and deformation-based pipelines, and naturally yields bijectivity and high coverage.

Cross-representation generality is convincingly demonstrated: the same pipeline applies to meshes, point clouds, SDFs, tetrahedral volumes, and inter-representation matching, which is a genuine practical advantage over spectral methods; a new SDF-based FAUST benchmark is a useful community contribution.

The empirical study is reasonably comprehensive: four standard benchmarks (FAUST, SMAL, SHREC20, KINECT), multiple metrics (Euclidean, geodesic, Dirichlet, coverage), and a wide range of baselines spanning axiomatic and learning-based paradigms. The method is competitive or superior on accuracy and consistently strong on coverage.

The comparison against Geomdist (Table 2) is honest and informative, isolating the benefit of flow matching over diffusion-based anchoring with quantitative divergence and accuracy evidence, and the paper clearly delineates the technical differences.
Beyond matching, downstream applications (SMPL-X scan fitting/skinning, UV parametrization, volumetric matching) demonstrate the versatility of the representation as claimed.
Limitations are discussed candidly (non-smooth maps, degraded point-cloud performance, landmark sensitivity), which strengthens scientific credibility.
weaknesses: The 'zero-shot' framing is overstated: each shape still requires training its own flow model, and the method relies on a small set of manually chosen landmarks per shape to build geodesic embeddings. This is effectively per-shape supervised initialization, weakening the claimed advantage over axiomatic pipelines (which also use landmarks/spectral descriptors) and limiting scalability to large collections.

Raw FUSE does not clearly dominate: on FAUST, plain KNN, FMaps-WKS, ZO, and NAM all achieve better Euclidean/geodesic accuracy than 'Ours', and KNN-IN-GAUSS outperforms FUSE on accuracy for the non-isometric datasets. The headline results (Ours-ZO, Ours-NAM) require pairwise refinement optimization, which partially contradicts the motivation of avoiding per-pair optimization.

The maps produced lack smoothness (noticeably higher Dirichlet energy than functional-map baselines), attributed to the non-smooth flow inversion; this is acknowledged but not resolved, and may limit adoption for geometry-processing tasks requiring smooth maps.

Comparison with modern data-driven matching methods is missing: the baselines are mostly axiomatic (FM variants, ZoomOut, NAM, NDP, OT). Recent unsupervised/supervised learned matchers (e.g., spectral-competitive learned descriptors, matching transformers) that typically surpass axiomatic methods are not included, so 'state-of-the-art' claims should be softened.

Several implementation details relevant to reproducibility (flow network architecture, training time/cost per shape, number of samples, timestep/ODE solver, landmark robustness) are deferred or unclear; robustness to landmark placement and to sampling density is not analyzed.

Typographical/consistency issues (e.g., 'coordindates', 'architechtures', 'gedesics', 'intoduced', notation ψ^l vs ψ^ℓ) and a few vague statements suggest the manuscript would benefit from careful proofreading.

strengths: Novel and clean conceptual contribution: representing maps between shapes as the composition of independently trained invertible flow-matching models through a shared Gaussian anchor is an original probabilistic alternative to functional maps, optimal transport, and template-based matching.

Genuinely modality-agnostic: the method requires only surface sampling and pointwise embeddings, and this is substantiated with experiments across meshes, point clouds, SDFs, inter-representation pairs, and volumetric tetrahedral meshes — a broader class of settings than most shape matching papers address.

Comprehensive experimental study: four standard benchmarks (FAUST, SMAL, SHREC20, KINECT), a newly introduced SDF-based FAUST benchmark, applications (SMPL-X fitting/skinning, UV parameterization, volume matching), and extensive ablations covering embedding choice (Tab. 2, Fig. 14), anchor distributions (Tab. 10), solver/steps (Tab. 11), landmark robustness (Fig. 4), and a careful FM vs. DDIM comparison with quantitative divergence evidence (Tab. 3, Fig. 11).

Transparent and honest analysis: the paper clearly discusses when FUSE fails (high-frequency embeddings, point-cloud-only matching, symmetry ambiguity), the non-bijectivity introduced by the KNN step, and the smoothness limitations of the obtained maps.
Strong empirical accuracy in the landmark-based regime, particularly on non-isometric pairs (SHREC20, SMAL) and for SDF matching where refinement baselines (ZoomOut, NAM) are inapplicable.
Practical efficiency: ~2 minutes and <2GB GPU memory per shape flow, with favorable inference time compared to refined baselines (Tab. 8); code promised for release.
weaknesses: The prior assumptions are strong and somewhat underplayed in the abstract/intro: the primary embedding (GFE) relies on 5-6 hand-picked landmarks on one shape, transferred to the rest of the dataset via ground truth correspondences. This is a non-trivial supervision signal, and the comparison to ULRSSM/Diff3F (different priors) in Tab. 1 and Tab. 4 should be interpreted with care despite the authors' acknowledgment.

FUSE is not state-of-the-art on the standard near-isometric benchmarks (ULRSSM substantially outperforms it on FAUST and SMAL in Tab. 4), and even among landmark-based geodesic methods the plain FUSE results are frequently surpassed by FMaps-ZO/NAM; the strongest results come from using FUSE as an initializer for these existing refinement schemes, which dilutes the standalone contribution.

The construction inherits a tension between claims and reality: the flow composition is invertible by design, but the final nearest-neighbor retrieval (Eq. 3) breaks bijectivity, and the resulting maps have notably higher Dirichlet energy than functional-map-based competitors — the main practical benefit of invertibility (coverage) is only partially realized.

The 'curse of frequency' limitation is significant: FUSE degrades with high-frequency embeddings (Tab. 2, Fig. 14), meaning the method works well mainly with low-dimensional smooth landmark geodesic embeddings, restricting the promised integration with rich learned features to future work (smoothed ULRSSM gains are modest: 0.082 to 0.068 in Tab. 9).

The method's heavy reliance on accurate geodesic distances and uniform surface sampling limits effectiveness on raw point clouds (KINECT results are weaker than NDP), tempering the representation-agnostic claim.

The theoretical justification for why independent flows compose into a meaningful correspondence (Sec. 4.2) is largely heuristic/empirical; the argument via Theorem 2 of [27] establishes marginal consistency of flows but does not formally characterize when the composition yields semantically correct matches.

Some editorial issues: an incomplete sentence in Sec. 4 ('The complete source code is available at'), repeated citation of Fig. 3, and minor typos (e.g., 'coordindates', 'transfered'), which slightly reduce polish.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel in the shape-matching literature: representing a per-shape map as an invertible flow from a shared Gaussian anchor and composing two flows to obtain a cross-shape correspondence is an elegant probabilistic alternative to functional maps, optimal transport, and registration-based pipelines, and the paper convincingly positions it against these paradigms.

The representation-agnostic property is demonstrated beyond surface meshes: matching across meshes, point clouds, SDFs, and volumetric tetrahedral meshes, with a new SDF-based FAUST benchmark (Tab. 5) where no prior quantitative evaluation exists — a tangible contribution for the community.

Experiments are broad and multi-faceted: four standard benchmarks, a diverse baseline set spanning axiomatic (FMaps, ZoomOut, NAM, WKS), OT-based, data-driven (ULRSSM), and foundation-model (Diff3F) approaches, plus four metrics including coverage and Dirichlet energy. The paper is candid about where it loses (ULRSSM on FAUST/SMAL, NDP on point clouds).

The analysis sections add value beyond the headline numbers: the 'curse of frequency' observation linking embedding Dirichlet energy to flow alignability (Tab. 2, Fig. 14), the controlled comparison of FM vs. DDIM inversion justifying the choice over GeomDist (Tab. 3, supplementary derivation), ablations over anchors, solvers, and landmark count, and FUSE used as a better-than-FMaps initialization for ZoomOut/NAM.

Practical efficiency: per-shape flow training takes ~2 minutes on a single consumer GPU with <2GB memory (supplementary), and no pairwise optimization is needed at test time. Code and full implementation details (architecture, training regime, baselines' configurations) are provided, supporting reproducibility.

The limitations section is substantive and honest: dependency of symmetry disambiguation on the embedding, reliance on consistent geodesics (excluding partial matching), and the non-bijective KNN retrieval step.
weaknesses: There is a tension between the headline framing and the actual method: the paper advertises an 'invertible' representation of maps, yet the final correspondence (Eq. 3) is a KNN step that is not bijective and the obtained maps have notably higher Dirichlet energy (worse smoothness) than FMaps-based baselines across all datasets. The continuous, fully bijective map the formulation suggests is deferred to future work, so the elegant theoretical property is not fully cashed out in practice.

The comparison against the strongest learned baselines is mixed: ULRSSM substantially outperforms FUSE on FAUST (0.0092 vs. 0.0289 Euclidean error) and SMAL. FUSE's advantage is concentrated on SHREC20 (where ULRSSM fails) and on scenarios where other methods cannot operate (SDFs, cross-representation). This is a defensible niche, but the claim of 'high, if not the highest, accuracy on various benchmarks' overstates the standard-benchmark standing.

The method requires manually selected landmarks on one shape per dataset, transferred via ground-truth correspondences, plus accurate geodesic distance computations. This is a fairly strong form of prior, and the paper's comparisons restrict the field to landmark-based methods, which weakens the practical significance relative to increasingly unsupervised or foundation-model-based pipelines.

On raw point clouds (KINECT, Tab. 4, and supplementary Tab. 7), FUSE is clearly the weaker option: it degrades relative to extrinsic methods like NDP and even relative to its own anchor-space variant in some regimes. Since modality-agnosticism is a central selling point, the reliance on reliable geodesics and uniform surface sampling is a substantive limitation for the noisier representations the paper targets.

The methodological novelty, while clean, is thin at its core: flow matching to a shared anchor and composing flows is a direct combination of existing machinery (CFM of Lipman et al.; the distribution-based shape representation of Geometry Distributions, which the authors acknowledge). The paper's value rests mostly on the insight of operating in an intrinsic feature space and the empirical validation, rather than on new theory; the supporting argument (independence of FM solutions from training couplings, via Theorem 2 of [27]) is informal.

Some results are under-analyzed: why FUSE ANCHOR beats FUSE in accuracy on non-isometric pairs at the cost of coverage is attributed qualitatively to inversion non-smoothness without deeper investigation; the newly introduced SDF benchmark lacks ground truth for correspondence beyond projected mesh vertices, and the topology-filtering criterion ('all shapes whose SDFs preserve valid topology') leaves room for selection effects.

Minor presentation issues: an incomplete sentence ('The complete source code is available at'), a duplicated figure reference ('as shown in Fig. 3 Fig. 3'), and typos ('coordindates', 'this measure the this measure') suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: FUSE recasts shape correspondence as a composition of invertible flow-matching models through a shared Gaussian anchor, offering a genuinely different representation of maps compared to the dominant functional-map, OT, and registration-based paradigms.

Strong modality-agnostic design: since only surface sampling and pointwise embeddings are required, the method applies uniformly to meshes, point clouds, SDFs, and volumetric (tetrahedral) data, and supports cross-representation matching — an underexplored capability demonstrated in Fig. 7 and Table 7.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across FAUST, SMAL, SHREC20, and KINECT, with multiple metrics (Euclidean/geodesic error, Dirichlet energy, coverage), a broad set of baselines spanning axiomatic and learned methods, and detailed supplementary ablations (anchor distributions, ODE solvers/steps, embedding smoothness/Dirichlet 'curse of frequency' analysis).

Thoughtful analysis of when and why the method works: the discussion of marginal-field uniqueness (Theorem 2 of [27]), the controlled FM-vs-DDIM inversion study (Table 3, Fig. 11, and the supplementary derivation), and the embedding-smoothness analysis provide insight rather than just benchmark numbers.

Practical efficiency: per-shape flow training takes ~2 minutes on a single GPU with <2GB memory, and maps between any pair of shapes are obtained with no per-pair optimization; FUSE also serves as a strong initializer for ZoomOut and NAM, yielding state-of-the-art results on SHREC20.

Clear, honest limitations section (symmetry disambiguation depends on the embedding, geodesic reliance limits point clouds/partial matching, non-bijective KNN retrieval), plus applicability beyond matching (scan fitting/skinning, UV parametrization, volumetric matching).
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is informal and somewhat overclaimed: the argument that flows coincide whenever E(S1)=E(S2) relies on uniqueness of the marginal velocity field, but the learned flow (not just the field) is not uniquely determined by the marginals in general, and FM solutions are known to depend on the couplings. A more careful treatment or empirical stress-testing of this claim would strengthen the paper; similarly, the claimed 'invertibility' of the overall map is weakened by the final non-bijective KNN retrieval step.

The method relies on a nontrivial prior: 5–6 landmarks are manually placed and transferred via ground-truth correspondences. While the paper frames this fairly and compares against other prior-based methods, the accuracy gains over prior-free or weaker-prior baselines should be read with this in mind, and the sensitivity to landmark placement, though studied, is only on selected datasets.

FUSE is not the strongest method everywhere: ULRSSM substantially outperforms it on FAUST/SMAL, NDP is better on point clouds, and FUSE maps have higher Dirichlet energy (less smoothness) than functional-map methods. The paper attributes these gaps reasonably, but the contribution is more 'competitive and more general' than 'state of the art across the board'.

Dependence on reliable geodesic distances and uniform surface sampling is a substantive limitation for real-world scanned point clouds (noise, partiality), and the paper does not evaluate any partial or noisy real-scan scenario beyond KINECT.

Presentation issues: an incomplete sentence in Section 4 ('The complete source code is available at' with no URL), a duplicated figure reference ('Fig. 3 Fig. 3'), and key implementation details (architecture, training time, landmark selection) relegated to the supplementary rather than the main text. These do not undermine the science but reduce polish.

No theoretical or empirical analysis of failure modes regarding embedding distribution mismatch severity (e.g., how far apart E(S1) and E(S2) can be before the flow composition fails), which would help practitioners decide when to apply FUSE.
